back: Replace old instances with new ones in batches so some capacity always serves traffic. The Kubernetes Deployment default.

front: maxSurge and maxUnavailable defaults in Kubernetes?
back: Both 25%. maxSurge rounds up (pods above desired), maxUnavailable rounds down (pods below desired).

front: 20 pods, maxSurge 5, maxUnavailable 0, 60 s per pod to become ready. Rollout time?
back: 4 waves of 5 × 60 s ≈ 4 minutes, needing 25% extra capacity (25 pods at peak).
Readiness failure removes the pod from Service endpoints. Liveness failure restarts the container.
Two full environments; deploy to the idle one, test it, switch all traffic at once, keep the old one for instant rollback.
Both colours share the database, so the schema must work for both versions. It also needs double capacity.
Send a small share of real traffic to the new version, compare its health with the old, and widen in steps or abort.

front: Canary blast radius: 600,000 users/hour, 5% canary, 10 minutes?
back: 100,000 users active in 10 minutes × 5% = about 5,000 users exposed.

front: Why compare a canary against a fresh baseline?
back: Old long-running pods differ (warm caches, process age). A same-size baseline of v1 deployed alongside isolates the version difference. Kayenta's approach.

front: Why route a canary by user hash, not by request?
back: So each user consistently sees one version instead of flickering between old and new on every request.
Release toggles, experiment toggles, ops toggles (kill switches) and permission toggles.

front: What does a feature flag separate?
back: Deploying code from releasing behaviour. Code ships dark; the flag decides who sees it, without a deploy.
Run new code on real production traffic without showing users its results, for example by mirroring requests and discarding responses.
Side effects: mirrored writes can charge cards, send emails or change shared data unless downstreams are stubbed.
Expand the schema to support old and new code, migrate data and readers, then contract by removing the old shape once unused.

front: Why can a fast ALTER TABLE cause an outage in PostgreSQL?
back: It needs an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock. Waiting behind a long query, it blocks every new query on the table. Set lock_timeout and retry.
